storyline.arc: It started as a tmux-ish terminal wrapper so you could watch Claude work inside a git worktree. Now it's a cross-platform tool with an MSI installer, a dashboard, a learning page, and a --backtrace mode that reconstructs coding history it wasn't around for.

eras.blurb: Embedded terminal, then Claude and OpenCode side by side, then LLM summaries so commits explain themselves and a bubblewrap sandbox so they can't wander off.
eras.title: Two backends and a summarizer

eras.blurb: aGiT became aGiTrack, session sharing learned to ask twice about sensitive data, and the whole thing grew per-session merge branches, sub-agent token accounting, and Esc that actually goes back.
eras.title: The rename, and consent forms

eras.blurb: A native Windows port with an MSI pipeline, plus a pre-commit hook to stop the agent committing to the base repo, which tells you how that had been going.
eras.title: Windows, and a guard against itself

eras.blurb: Cover commits with a watermark that survives, proxy mode renamed to interactive, and --backtrace to rebuild coding history from repos that never had aGiTrack running.
eras.title: Background mode and time travel

eras.blurb: A learning page joins the dashboard as a static export, daemons learn to survive restarts, and several rounds of fixing token counts that had been quietly wrong.
eras.title: Dashboards, daemons, and counting properly

moments.detail: The trail started with a plain report: summaries just weren't showing up in interactive no-worktree mode, and the answer to "are you sure?" was "please create a dummy repository and test it yourself." It turned out the staging prompt in auto mode was returning early, so runner.py never got around to the summary, and auto-fold would happily commit while a summary was still pending. The fix makes auto-fold wait for those pending summaries before committing, with test_summary_async.py added to keep it honest.
moments.summary: A staging prompt in auto mode was swallowing the summary step nobody noticed was missing.

thoughts.note: Chasing a prompt that needed a second Enter to send, not yet knowing it was hiding a missing summary step.
thoughts.quote: In interactive no-worktree auto mode, when it asks for whether to stage some files and I choose unstage. It shows that the prompt is not sent due to user edits not committed. When I press enter again, it gets sent. It should send once I unstage the files, since there are no more files left after unstaging. Also, the agent should be still allowed to proceed even if the user edits are not committed, with a warning showing that all the changes will be committed once the agent finishes its run if in auto-commit mode (no warning needed for manual-commit mode).

thoughts.note: Realizing the commit was racing the summary, so auto-fold had to learn to wait.

moments.detail: The tell was a subagent: the main agent would sit there waiting for its child to finish, look perfectly idle to aGiTrack, and get interrupted with a commit prompt mid-thought. So idle detection stopped trusting appearances and started checking when the transcript file was last written, in agitrack/transcripts/claude.py and the backend check in proxy_agents.py. moments.detail: The whole week was a running argument with the daemon about *when* a turn is actually over: commits kept landing that had a user message and no agent reply, so the message described work the agent hadn't done yet. The fix in commit_engine.py and background.py stamps those with in-flight metadata instead, so a mid-turn commit still says which session and turn it came from rather than pretending nobody was home.

moments.detail: The user was using agitrack to develop agitrack, which means the daemon tracking their session and the agent editing the code were both reaching for the same state file at the same moment. One would truncate it mid-write, the other would read the wreckage, and the crash looked like a bug in the tool rather than the tool eating its own tail. The fix was a shared atomic write helper in agitrack/fileio.py, write to a temp file and rename, threaded through state.py, daemons.py and the metrics daemon so nobody sees a half-written file again.
moments.summary: Two copies of the tool writing the same file at once corrupted it; atomic writes ended the self-inflicted crash.

thoughts.note: They suspected the recursion was the cause before knowing the mechanism, and they were right: two writers, one file.
thoughts.quote: I got this error before while you were editing. Is it because I'm coding agitrack within agitrack? moments.detail: The trigger was mundane: after an aGiTrack update the daemons were supposed to restart themselves, and instead both dashboards just stopped. Turned out they were tied to whoever spawned them, so restart.py's exec-based handoff took them down with it; that got swapped for spawn-and-verify with a rollback, and daemon.py stopped assuming a live parent. The other half came from a good question about failure states: if a restart fails, the stop commands still need capturing and the corpse should still show up under -daemons instead of quietly vanishing.
moments.summary: Background processes learned to survive on their own instead of dying with whatever launched them.

thoughts.quote: That also means we still need to capture the stop commands even if restart failed, and a failed restarted daemon should still be visible via the -daemons option

thoughts.note: Both dashboards were dead after an update, so exec-and-hope became spawn, verify, and roll back if it didn't take.

moments.detail: The truncation fix only ran when a subject was written, so every backtrace entry already on disk kept its mid-word chop, and the cache quietly guaranteed those stale entries would keep being served. Ripping the cache out of agitrack/metrics/backtrace.py meant subjects got rebuilt from the source prompts on every read, which is when the numbers underneath stopped adding up: chasing why the token counts in commit messages didn't match the backtrace turned into three separate fixes, including a watermark in commit_engine.py that was re-exporting whole sessions after context loss.
moments.summary: Old backtrace logs kept their truncated subjects, which is how three separate token-counting bugs got noticed.

thoughts.note: Noticing the fix only applied going forward, and asking why a log that reads from disk needed a cache at all.
thoughts.quote: The fix I asked you about the backtrace log subject message seems not be applied to older messages - they still get truncated sometimes within a word and no dots indicating the truncation.

moments.detail: The complaint was simple: run the live dashboard and the backtrace dashboard on the same repo, same 24 hour window, and the token totals still disagreed. Turned out a few commits carried wildly inflated counts, so collect.py and insights.py learned to spot those outliers and leave them out of the totals rather than averaging the weirdness into everything. The follow-up was the fun part: rather than just hiding the bad numbers going forward, they ran git filter-branch over the affected range to rewrite the old commit messages with the corrected token counts.
moments.summary: The gap wasn't rounding: a handful of abnormal commits were skewing the totals until they were excluded.

thoughts.note: First they assumed the tracked-lines gap was a bug, then accepted backtrace mode simply can't see every edit an agent makes, and added a note saying so.

thoughts.note: The 24 hour filter had been the suspect; once it was ruled out, the remaining explanation was that some individual commits were just wrong.
thoughts.quote: What did you fix. When I run both dashboards on the current repo, I still see a big difference even with the 24 hours filter. The dashboard needs to detect abnormal commits and exclude/fix them in the token count. In addition, such abnormal commits should never happen again.

moments.detail: It started with a paste: multi-line text going into the backend agent's terminal, and aGiTrack reading some of those line breaks as Enter and cheerfully answering its own "new commits?" popup on the user's behalf. moments.detail: The want was simple enough: a page that reads the project's history back to you as a story, reachable from both the live dashboard and the backtrace one, with each using its own data. Getting there was less simple. The chain of thought kept cutting off mid-word, the acts summarized badly (one confidently announced Windows was finally in, about a month after Windows landed), and the fix for that was two rounds of ripping chapters back out in story.py until only the latest few showed at once.

storyline.tagline: Someone built a tracker for AI coding sessions, then used it to track the AI coding sessions building it, and the commit log is 773 messages of that snake eating its own tail.
